extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and practitioners of political philosophy and social science
extracted.subtask_description: Critically assessing methods for investigating social and political phenomena — when induction or deduction is appropriate, and the logical limits of experimental, geometrical, and deductive approaches in social science.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objective of the Social Science
rubrics_metrics.description: The science of society should enable us to understand, in any given condition of social affairs, by what causes it has been made what it is; whether it is tending to any changes and what; what effects each feature of its existing state is likely to produce in the future; and by what means any of those effects might be prevented, modified, or accelerated, or a different class of effects superinduced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The object is not necessarily precise long-range prediction but causal understanding sufficient for guidance in particular conditions; 'There is nothing chimerical in the hope that general laws... do really admit of being ascertained.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Social phenomena derive from individual human nature (Composition of Causes)
rubrics_metrics.description: All phenomena of society are phenomena of human nature, generated by the action of outward circumstances upon masses of human beings; human beings in society have no properties but those derived from the laws of individual human nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat social phenomena as composed of causes traceable to individual motives and circumstances; avoid treating social aggregates as a fundamentally different substance (no emergent substance with completely new properties).

rubrics_metrics.name: Inapplicability of pure experimental (chemical) method to social phenomena
rubrics_metrics.description: The chemical/experimental method (requiring controlled, repeatable experiments and elimination of other causes) cannot be successfully applied to social phenomena because we lack the means to make artificial experiments, cannot hold all other circumstances constant, and historical instances are not controlled experiments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arguments drawing general conclusions from single unanalyzed instances or casual historical examples are invalid; specific experience often cannot satisfy requisites for true induction in social matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement and impracticability of the Method of Difference
rubrics_metrics.description: The Method of Difference requires two instances which tally in every particular except the one under inquiry; this is manifestly impossible for nations or societies (e.g., two nations alike in all respects except commercial policy).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because legislative and institutional differences arise from prior differences, there are always innumerable other varying antecedents; therefore an 'experimentum crucis' of social policies cannot be obtained by simple between-nation comparison.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits of the Indirect Method of Difference (comparing classes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Comparing classes of instances that differ in the presence or absence of the circumstance (e.g., one restrictive nation vs several free-trade ones) still fails to establish causation because prosperity is usually the collective result of many favorable circumstances and a restrictive nation may simply combine more favorable causes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even carefully assembled class comparisons give only a specious semblance of conclusiveness; one cannot infer exclusivity of cause when effects are multicausal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weakness of the Method of Agreement under plurality of causes
rubrics_metrics.description: The Method of Agreement (finding one antecedent common to all cases sharing an effect) provides negligible presumption of causation when the effect admits of several causes, which is typical for social phenomena.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Eliminating other antecedents only shows the effect can sometimes occur without them, not that the remaining antecedent is the sole or principal cause; social effects almost always have multiple contributing causes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Failure of the Method of Concomitant Variations when causes co-act
rubrics_metrics.description: The Method of Concomitant Variations (linking proportional changes in antecedent and consequent) is ineffective because attributes of social bodies are influenced by innumerable causes whose effects mix nonlinearly; variations of aggregate measures will not bear a uniform proportion to any single component cause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because different causes do not produce effects of strictly different kinds and because of mutual interdependence among societal elements, concomitant variation reasoning misleads in social inquiry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role and limits of the Method of Residues
rubrics_metrics.description: The Method of Residues (accounting for effects by known causes and attributing the remainder to other known circumstances) presupposes that many causes are already known and thus is not a method of pure observation but of deduction supplemented by experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applied to social phenomena, residues require prior knowledge of the tendencies of some causes—knowledge that cannot be obtained by specific experience alone; thus deduction from principles of human nature is essential, with experience only to check or supplement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity of deduction from laws of human nature
rubrics_metrics.description: Because specific empirical methods cannot furnish all required causal knowledge, the social science must often be deductive, relying on principles derived from human nature to explain political tendencies and predict consequences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experimental evidence can only verify or supplement conclusions drawn from general laws of human motives; one must be willing to reason a priori about tendencies grounded in human nature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejection of the geometrical/abstract method (single-cause axiomatization)
rubrics_metrics.description: The geometrical or abstract method (treating social science like geometry, where propositions are universal and unaffected by other principles) is erroneous because social phenomena result from conjunctions and conflicts of many causes, unlike immutable geometric truths.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid modelling social science as a system where a single principle yields universally true conclusions regardless of other factors; unlike geometry, social laws interact and can modify or cancel one another's effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid basing political theory on unbending practical maxims or abstract right
rubrics_metrics.description: Deducing political conclusions from 'abstract right' or unbending maxim (or treating a social contract fiction as factual) mistakes practical precepts for theoretical foundations and confuses art and science.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rules of conduct must follow, not precede, ascertainment of laws; do not treat practical maxims as premises to build theoretical explanations without empirical/deductive justification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caution against single-cause 'interest-philosophy' explanations
rubrics_metrics.description: The Benthamite 'interest-philosophy' which assumes men's actions are always determined solely by private worldly interest (and hence that rulers act only from self-interest unless made accountable) is overly simplistic and false as a universal claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing collective or governmental behavior, account for other powerful influences: habitual sentiments, prevailing modes of thinking, class characteristics, traditions, maxims inherited from predecessors, and senses of duty or philanthropy—these can substantially shape rulers' conduct beyond mere self-interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Responsibility (accountability) is not the sole means to align rulers' interests with the governed
rubrics_metrics.description: The proposition that accountability to the governed is the only cause capable of producing identity of interest between rulers and the people is false; identity in essentials may arise from coinciding interests (e.g., rulers wishing to suppress anarchy) independently of responsibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze the multiple mechanisms that can align rulers' actions with public good (shared interests, historical traditions, common aims), and do not assume institutional responsibility is the exclusive or always-effective instrument.
